prose_changes.old: Gregory of Neocaesarea was a devoted pupil of Origen. In the 250s, some Christians looted with Gothic raiders. Gregory wrote a canonical letter, a letter of rules for the church, about them. It worked out what to do with them, case by case. Methodius of Olympus came a generation later. He turned Plato's Symposium into a Christian dialogue. In it, ten women take turns to praise chastity. He also became one of the first serious critics of Origen. Then he died in the persecution around 311.

prose_changes.old: In 268 or thereabouts, the bishops of Syria and Asia Minor met at Antioch to deal with their own metropolitan. It was the third time in a few years. Paul of Samosata was bishop of the greatest city in the Roman East. The council that removed him says he liked to be called ducenarius. That was a salaried official's title, probably held under the Palmyrene rulers of the city. The charges mix doctrine with deportment. He had a raised throne built for himself in church. He stopped the old hymns and had new ones sung to himself. Women in his household gave scandal. The teaching at issue was that Christ was a man in whom the Word had come to dwell. On this view, he was not the Word made flesh. The reading was later called adoptionist. The council could not make its removal of him stick. The civil power was Palmyrene, and Paul had its favor. He went only when Aurelian retook the city in 272. The emperor settled who owned the church building by asking which claimant was in communion with the bishops of Italy and Rome. It was the first time a Roman emperor ruled on a Christian dispute. The letter announcing the deposition was drafted by Malchion. He ran a school of rhetoric in the city. He had cross-examined Paul in front of shorthand writers. A generation later, in the same city, a presbyter named Lucian worked over the text of the Greek Bible. He taught a circle of students, Arius among them. Afterwards they used his name as a badge.

Paul of Samosata was bishop of the greatest city in the Roman East. The council that removed him says he liked to be called ducenarius, a salaried official's title, probably held under the Palmyrene rulers of the city. The charges mix doctrine with deportment. He had a raised throne built for himself in church, he stopped the old hymns and had new ones sung to himself, and women in his household gave scandal. The teaching at issue was that Christ was a man in whom the Word had come to dwell, not the Word made flesh. The reading was later called adoptionist. The council could not make its removal of him stick, because the civil power was Palmyrene and Paul had its favor. He went only when Aurelian retook the city in 272. The emperor settled who owned the church building by asking which claimant was in communion with the bishops of Italy and Rome. It was the first time a Roman emperor ruled on a Christian dispute. The letter announcing the deposition was drafted by Malchion, who ran a school of rhetoric in the city and had cross-examined Paul in front of shorthand writers. A generation later, in the same city, a presbyter named Lucian worked over the text of the Greek Bible. He taught a circle of students, Arius among them, who afterwards used his name as a badge.

prose_changes.old: Marian devotion in both East and West rests in large part on the Protevangelium of James. Anna and Joachim and the presentation in the Temple came from it into the church's calendar and its sacred images. Yet the church never accepted the book as scripture. The ox and the ass at the manger come from Pseudo-Matthew, a later Latin retelling. The apocryphal Acts tell how the apostles died: Peter crucified head down, Philip hung by his ankles. Medieval art and legend probably took most of what they knew of those deaths from them. And the Jewish books in this collection, written under the names of ancient figures, survive only because Christians copied them. The irony is plain. They were kept by the tradition that had parted from the one that produced them.

prose_changes.old: It sits between two neighbors. One is Latin pastoral Christianity at Carthage. It has the same language, but not the same region. The other is Homoian Christianity, which has the same region. Fifty years later, its leaders held sees in these provinces. Its own commentary on the Apocalypse comes to us as Jerome edited it.
prose_changes.new: It sits between two neighbors. One is Latin pastoral Christianity at Carthage, with the same language but not the same region. The other is Homoian Christianity, with the same region; fifty years later its leaders held sees in these provinces. This church's own bishop, Victorinus, wrote on the Apocalypse, and Jerome later put out his book again with a new ending.

prose_changes.old: Justin made a bold claim. Before the incarnation, he said, the Word was already sowing seeds of truth in the philosophers. That gave the church a way to deal with the learning it had inherited, and it has never fully put that down. Clement at Alexandria spoke the same way of philosophers receiving 'the seeds of the Truth'. He and Origen took the idea much further. The apologists also settled some of the church's words. Theophilus is the first writer whose work survives to use the word Trinity of God. And one line from the Epistle to Diognetus has outlived every other line the movement produced. It calls Christians resident aliens, at home everywhere and strangers everywhere.

prose_changes.old: Around 124 a Christian named Quadratus handed the emperor Hadrian a written defense of his religion. For the next eighty years, others kept doing the same. Aristides did it at Athens. Justin did it twice, and was put to death for it about 165. He was a philosopher who kept wearing the philosopher's cloak after his conversion, and he ran a school at Rome. Athenagoras addressed Marcus Aurelius, and so did Melito of Sardis. Theophilus wrote three books to a pagan friend named Autolycus. An unknown writer produced the letter to Diognetus, still the most quoted thing any of them wrote. The charges were always roughly the same, and so were the answers. Christians were called atheists because they had no images. They were called cannibals because of what they said about eating a body. And they were called disloyal because they would not sacrifice. What made the effort interesting was the second move. Several of them, Justin above all, did more than deny the charges. They argued that the best of Greek philosophy had been reaching toward what the church now held. Christians were therefore the true heirs of reason, not its enemies.

prose_changes.old: Mani was born in Mesopotamia in 216. He was raised in a sect of baptizers. He broke with it after what he described as revelations from his heavenly twin. He taught that reality is the battleground of two principles, Light and Darkness, which have both always existed. Particles of light are trapped in the material world. A strict discipline of self-denial sets them free. Almost alone among founders of his era, he wrote his own scriptures. He also had them translated on purpose. He meant his faith to absorb and replace Christianity, Zoroastrianism and Buddhism at once. For a time, it worked. The faith spread from Persia across the Roman Empire. It also spread east along the Silk Road into Central Asia and China. His followers divided into two groups. The Elect kept the full discipline. The Hearers supported them and lived ordinary lives. Augustine of Hippo was a Hearer for roughly nine years before his conversion. He spent much of his later career arguing against the teachers he had once sat under. Mani himself died in custody under the Persian king Bahram I in the 270s.

prose_changes.old: Marcion was a wealthy shipowner from Sinope. He concluded that the God of the Hebrew Scriptures was strict and gave the law. The Father whom Jesus revealed was merciful. To Marcion, these could not be the same being. The Roman church expelled him and gave back his money. By tradition, this happened in 144. He then built a rival network of churches with its own edited Scripture. It held a version of Luke and ten letters of Paul. He had stripped them of what he judged to be Jewish corruption.
prose_changes.new: Marcion was a wealthy shipowner from Sinope. He concluded that the strict God of the Hebrew Scriptures, who gave the law, could not be the same being as the merciful Father whom Jesus revealed. The Roman church expelled him and gave back his money, by tradition in 144. He then built a rival network of churches with its own edited Scripture: a version of Luke and ten letters of Paul, which he had stripped of what he judged to be Jewish corruption.

prose_changes.old: No church descends from the New Prophecy. In the sixth century, under Justinian, the empire moved to crush it. Procopius says the Montanists of Phrygia shut themselves in their churches and set them alight. Its own writings were destroyed. What remains is a handful of quoted oracles. There are also inscriptions on graves in Phrygia. But whether they are Montanist is itself argued over. That is the honest problem. Almost all the surviving evidence comes through two sources: the three named prophets, and their enemies. Does the community's own voice survive anywhere? That is not yet settled. What outlasted the movement are the questions it forced. Did prophecy go on after the apostles? Who may authorize it? How does a church tell genuine inspiration from enthusiasm? Critics of later revivals have reached for the comparison. In 1743 Charles Chauncy likened the cries and falling down of the Great Awakening to the Montanists of old. No line of descent links any later movement to it.

They read aloud from the prophets and from the apostles' memoirs. And they shared the bread and the cup, either in a full common meal or as the bread and wine alone.

prose_changes.old: No community descends from him — there is some evidence of a small group of followers in Carthage after his death, and nothing beyond that. His legacy is linguistic and rhetorical: the Latin words for the Trinity, and lines that entered the common speech of Christianity, most famously his claim that the blood of Christians is seed. Cyprian, Jerome and Augustine all read him closely, and the Western habit of thinking about God, the church and the sacraments in legal and forensic categories owes a great deal to a man who was never canonized and never quite belonged anywhere.
prose_changes.new: No community descends from him. There is some evidence of a small group of followers in Carthage after his death, and nothing beyond that. His legacy lies in words and rhetoric. He gave Latin its words for the Trinity, and lines that entered the common speech of Christians, most famously his claim that the blood of Christians is seed. Cyprian and Jerome read him closely, and Augustine called his many works eloquent and still read. The Western habit of thinking about God, the church and the sacraments in legal terms owes a great deal to him. Yet he was never made a saint, and he never quite belonged anywhere.
